introduction.heading: What is TypeScript?
introduction.description: TypeScript is JavaScript with a type system layered on top. You describe the shape data should have - a string, a User with an id and a name, a function that takes two numbers - and the TypeScript compiler checks that your code actually matches those shapes before it ever runs. Every valid JavaScript file is already valid TypeScript; you opt into stricter checking incrementally, one file or one annotation at a time.

concepts.title: Static Typing
concepts.description: Types are checked while you write code, not while it runs - a mismatched type is a red squiggle in your editor, not a 2am production error

concepts.title: Type Inference
concepts.description: TypeScript figures out most types on its own from the value you assign - you only annotate where it can't guess or where being explicit helps

concepts.title: Interfaces & Type Aliases
concepts.description: Name the shape of an object once with interface or type, then reuse that name anywhere the shape applies

concepts.title: Structural Typing
concepts.description: A value matches a type if its shape matches, regardless of what it was declared as - TypeScript checks the fields you have, not the label on the box

concepts.title: Generics
concepts.description: Write a function or type once with a placeholder type parameter like <T>, and let each call site fill in the real type

concepts.title: Compiling to JavaScript
concepts.description: The TypeScript compiler (tsc) strips the types away and outputs plain JavaScript - types exist only at compile time, with zero runtime cost

typeChecking.heading: Catching Bugs Before Runtime
typeChecking.description: In plain JavaScript, passing the wrong kind of value to a function is usually silent until something breaks - maybe immediately, maybe three steps later, maybe only for one particular user. TypeScript moves that check earlier: it walks through your code without running it and flags any place a value doesn't match what a type expects, right in your editor and again when you try to compile.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Install TypeScript into a project with npm install --save-dev typescript
Run npx tsc --init to generate a tsconfig.json with sensible defaults
Rename .js files to .ts (or .jsx to .tsx for files with JSX) to opt them into type checking
Run npx tsc to compile, or use a build tool (Vite, esbuild, webpack) that compiles TypeScript for you
Turn on "strict": true in tsconfig.json as early as you can - it catches far more than the defaults
Adopt it incrementally in an existing JS codebase with "allowJs": true and "checkJs": true before converting files outright

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A typed function working with an interface and a generic helper
fullExample.description: This ties the core concepts above together in one realistic file: an interface describing a shape, a function typed against it, and a small generic helper reused for something unrelated. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.
code: dueDate?: string; // optional - not every task has one
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: T[], key: K): T[K][] {
{ id: 2, title: "Ship it", done: true, dueDate: "2026-09-01" },

steps.label: Describe the shape
steps.explanation: interface Task names a shape once: every Task has an id, a title, and a done flag. The ? on dueDate marks it optional - a Task is still valid without it.

steps.label: Type a function's parameter
steps.explanation: task: Task means only an object matching that shape can be passed in - calling formatTask("hello") would be a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

steps.label: Handle an optional field safely
steps.explanation: Because dueDate is typed as string | undefined, TypeScript won't let you use it without first checking it's there - the ternary here is that check.

steps.label: Write a generic helper
steps.explanation: T is "whatever type of item is in the array" and K extends keyof T restricts key to an actual property name on T - so pluck(tasks, "nope") would fail to compile.

steps.label: Type an array of objects
steps.explanation: Task[] means every element in the array is checked against the Task shape - leaving out title, for example, would be flagged right here.

steps.label: Let inference do the rest
steps.explanation: pluck's return type isn't written anywhere - TypeScript works out T[K][] from how pluck is called, so tasks.title lines up with string[] and tasks.done with boolean[] automatically.
